study_sequence.directive: Specify the field over which a vector space is defined (typically ℝ or ℂ) and explain how scalars act via scalar multiplication, including how changing the field changes what counts as a vector space.
State the axioms (addition, scalar multiplication, and their properties) that define a vector space over a field, and be able to verify whether a given set with operations satisfies them.
Work through the main examples (e.g., F^n, function spaces, polynomial spaces) and explicitly identify the vectors, scalars, and operations in each example.
Define subspace and apply the closure conditions (under addition and scalar multiplication) to determine whether a subset of a vector space is a subspace.
Define linear combination and span, compute spans of given sets, and interpret span as the smallest subspace containing a set.
Define linear independence via the uniqueness of representing 0 as a linear combination, and determine whether a given list of vectors is independent or dependent using the defining equation.
State and use the definition of a basis (a list that is linearly independent and spans), and be able to verify that a given list is (or is not) a basis.
Given a basis, write vectors uniquely as linear combinations of basis vectors and interpret the resulting scalars as coordinates.
Define dimension as the length of any basis, and apply basic consequences (e.g., comparisons via spanning/independence and existence of bases in finite-dimensional spaces).
Define what it means for a vector space to be finite-dimensional (existence of a finite spanning list) and be able to decide in examples whether a space is finite- or infinite-dimensional.
Use linear combinations to express vectors in terms of a spanning list and apply finite-dimensional spanning arguments (including how spanning interacts with subspaces).
Use finite-dimensional tools (spanning lists, bases, and dimension) to analyze subspaces, including generating/identifying bases of subspaces and comparing dimensions.
Present and use the relationship between dimensions of the domain, null space, and range (rank–nullity), and apply it to deduce injectivity/surjectivity consequences in finite dimensions.
State the definition of a linear map between vector spaces (preservation of addition and scalar multiplication) and give a few representative examples and non-examples.
Explain how a linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces is represented by a matrix once bases are chosen, and how to compute/apply that matrix to coordinate vectors.
Define the null space (kernel) of a linear map and explain how it characterizes injectivity, including how to test injectivity using the null space.
Define the range (image) of a linear map and explain surjectivity in terms of the range, including how to test surjectivity.
Define composition of linear maps and inverse maps when they exist, and state the criteria for invertibility in terms of injectivity/surjectivity (especially in finite dimensions).
Define the characteristic polynomial and relate its roots to eigenvalues; include how it depends on a chosen basis/matrix representation and what is basis-independent about it.
Define the minimal polynomial of an operator (or matrix), prove it exists in finite dimensions, and use it to deduce algebraic relations satisfied by the operator.
State and use the division algorithm for polynomials (existence and uniqueness of quotient and remainder) and demonstrate it with worked examples.
Define p(T) for a linear map/operator T and a polynomial p, and show how this construction behaves with respect to addition, scalar multiplication, and composition of operators.

Define the vector space of polynomials over a field, including degree and the standard basis {1, x, x^2, …}, and illustrate how polynomial addition and scalar multiplication fit the vector space axioms.
Explain the relationship between a polynomial’s zeros and its linear factors, including how multiplicity is reflected in repeated factors.
Define the characteristic polynomial of a linear map/matrix, explain how its zeros are eigenvalues, and define algebraic multiplicity.
State and use the criterion for when an operator/matrix is diagonalizable (existence of a basis of eigenvectors) and show how diagonal form represents the action of the operator.
Define the eigenspace corresponding to an eigenvalue and prove it is a subspace; relate eigenvectors to the null space of a shifted operator.
Define eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a linear map (operator) and explain how to verify the eigenvector/eigenvalue equation and interpret it geometrically.
Define geometric multiplicity as the dimension of an eigenspace and relate it to algebraic multiplicity using dimension arguments and null space/range relationships.
Explain why the eigenvalues of an upper/lower triangular matrix are the diagonal entries and use this to find eigenvalues efficiently in examples.
State the definition of an inner product on a vector space (over R or C), list the axioms it satisfies, and give standard examples (especially on F^n).
Define the norm and distance coming from an inner product and record the key inequalities (especially Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality) that justify these definitions.
Define orthogonality, orthonormal sets, and orthonormal bases; include the basic consequences for linear independence and for computing coordinates/lengths.
Present the Gram–Schmidt procedure and its output; explain what input it requires (a basis or linearly independent list) and what it produces (an orthonormal basis for the same span).

Define the orthogonal complement of a subspace and the orthogonal projection onto a subspace; state the key decomposition result (vector equals projection plus orthogonal remainder) and the associated minimization/closest-point property.
State and use the representation of linear functionals via inner products (each functional equals inner product with a unique vector), and indicate how it depends on orthonormal bases.

Define the adjoint T* of a linear operator T on an inner product space and state its characterizing property. Include core identities and how to compute T* from inner-product data / matrices in an orthonormal basis.

Define normal operators (commuting with their adjoint) and develop the standard consequences emphasized in the chapter (orthogonal eigenspaces, diagonalizability in the complex case deferred/linked to later results).
Define orthogonal (real) and unitary (complex) operators and relate them to preserving inner products and norms. State equivalent characterizations (e.g., T*T=I) and main structural consequences.

Define self-adjoint operators and record their key spectral properties used later (e.g., real eigenvalues, orthogonality of eigenvectors). Provide the main theorems that describe their behavior in finite-dimensional inner product spaces.

State the spectral theorem in the form used by the text (existence of an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors / diagonal matrix in an orthonormal basis). Indicate how it is applied to analyze operators on inner product spaces.
Define positive operators via ⟨Tv,v⟩≥0 and develop the associated tools highlighted in the chapter (ordering, functional consequences, existence/uniqueness of positive square roots when applicable).
State and use the result that every linear operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space has an eigenvalue, and explain how this follows from polynomial roots.
Present the Schur form for operators on complex inner product spaces (especially normal operators), including the role of an orthonormal basis and the unitary change of basis.
State and apply the spectral theorem that a normal operator on a complex inner product space is diagonalizable by an orthonormal basis.
Define how to interpret p(T) for a polynomial p and a normal operator T using diagonalization, and connect the resulting eigenvalues of p(T) to p evaluated on eigenvalues of T.
Explain conditions under which a family (or pair) of commuting normal operators can be diagonalized in a single orthonormal basis, and how this is used.
Describe how to build a basis in which an operator has an upper-triangular matrix, and specify what the diagonal entries represent.
Define k-linear (multilinear) maps on a product of vector spaces, give key examples, and state the basic algebraic properties (linearity in each slot, behavior under fixing variables).

Construct the tensor product (or characterize it via its universal property) so that multilinear maps correspond to linear maps out of a tensor product; use this to define and manipulate tensors and tensor powers.
Define alternating multilinear forms, build the exterior power using the alternating projection (or quotient construction), and develop the wedge product and its core identities.

Define the determinant as the unique alternating multilinear function of the columns (or rows) normalized to be 1 on the identity, and derive standard properties (multiplicativity, effect of row operations, det(A)=0 iff not invertible).
Relate determinant and trace (and possibly other coefficients) to the characteristic polynomial, and show how these quantities behave under change of basis and similarity.
Explain how determinants encode oriented volume scaling (and orientation change) of linear maps; connect this to geometric interpretations in real inner-product spaces.
